import { CardGrid, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This page collects the load-bearing details behind the SDK's convenience
macros: what `#[derive(Mergeable)]` actually generates, why a value stored in a
map needs deterministic ids, how private state is stored, and the rules for
xcalls, handlers and migrations. If you have only written apps with the derive
macros and the built-in collections, you do not need any of this — reach for it
when you hand-roll a collection value, store private state, or write a
non-trivial migration.

On a cluster an app's calls run one at a time on its leader and the other
replicas apply what each run wrote; nothing is merged between replicas
([CRDT collections](/protocol/crdt-internals/)). The `Mergeable` machinery below
is what the storage crate requires of a value's type, not what keeps replicas
in agreement.

Prerequisites: [`collections`](/build/collections/) and
[`sdk-macros`](/build/sdk-macros/).

## Custom `Mergeable` for a struct value

A struct stored as a collection value (e.g. `UnorderedMap<String, TeamStats>`)
must implement `Mergeable`; the collections require it of their values. The
trait is small:

```rust
pub trait Mergeable {
    fn merge(&mut self, other: &Self) -> Result<(), MergeError>;
}
```

The simplest path is `#[derive(Mergeable)]`, which calls `merge` on every field.
You hand-write the impl only when you need custom behavior (validation, logging,
business rules, skipping a field). A hand-rolled impl that delegates
field-by-field to each `Counter`:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Default, BorshSerialize, BorshDeserialize)]
#[borsh(crate = "calimero_sdk::borsh")]
pub struct TeamStats {
    pub wins: Counter,
    pub losses: Counter,
    pub draws: Counter,
}

impl Mergeable for TeamStats {
    fn merge(&mut self, other: &Self) -> Result<(), MergeError> {
        // Custom hooks go here (validation, logging, business rules);
        // then delegate to each field's own merge.
        self.wins.merge(&other.wins)?;
        self.losses.merge(&other.losses)?;
        self.draws.merge(&other.draws)?;
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

The team-metrics app showed this (with a `badges |= other.badges` rule) on
this SDK until it moved to the component SDK as `apps/team-metrics`, where one Raft log orders every
call and there is no merge to write: its `award_badge` reads the current mask
and sets a bit, so concurrent awards both land. Its doc comment says what
replaced the merge rule.

`#[derive(Mergeable)]` works on **structs only** (every field must itself be
`Mergeable`). For an **enum**, wrap it in `LwwRegister<MyEnum>` instead of
deriving.

## A hand-rolled `Mergeable` also needs `RekeyTarget`

This is the part that bites. `merge` alone is not enough: a struct stored as a
map **value** has nested collection fields (`Counter`, `LwwRegister`, …) that
each carry their own entity id. For those fields to be stored as child entities
of the entry, under ids that follow from the entry's key rather than from a
random draw, each must be re-keyed. That is what `RekeyTarget` does: it re-keys
each field under a deterministic, field-namespaced child of the parent entry's
id.

`#[derive(Mergeable)]` generates **both** the `Mergeable` impl *and* the
`RekeyTarget` impl. When you write `Mergeable` by hand you must also write
`RekeyTarget` by hand:

```rust
impl calimero_storage::collections::rekey::RekeyTarget for TeamStats {
    fn rekey_relative_to(&mut self, parent_id: calimero_storage::address::Id) {
        use calimero_storage::collections::rekey::field_child_id;
        calimero_storage::rekey_field_if_supported!(
            &mut self.wins,
            field_child_id(parent_id, "wins")
        );
        calimero_storage::rekey_field_if_supported!(
            &mut self.losses,
            field_child_id(parent_id, "losses")
        );
        calimero_storage::rekey_field_if_supported!(
            &mut self.draws,
            field_child_id(parent_id, "draws")
        );
    }
}
```

Skip `RekeyTarget` and the nested fields keep the random ids they were born
with. Always pair a hand-written `Mergeable` with a hand-written `RekeyTarget`
(one `field_child_id(parent_id, "field")` per nested field), or just
`#[derive(Mergeable)]` and get both for free.

## Storage strategy: `Blob` vs `Structured`

Every collection type declares a `StorageStrategy`, which decides whether a
nested value is stored as one entity or as several:

```rust
pub enum StorageStrategy {
    /// Store as one opaque blob (leaf CRDTs).
    Blob,
    /// Store fields separately with composite keys (containers).
    Structured,
}
```

| Strategy | Types | Stored as |
|----------|-------|------------|
| `Blob` | `Counter`, `LwwRegister` | the whole entry, one value |
| `Structured` | `UnorderedMap`, `Vector`, `UnorderedSet` | each child its own entity |

A `Blob` type is a leaf: a write rewrites it whole. A `Structured` type is a
container: its children are stored under composite keys, so a write touches only
the child it changes. That is what lets a counter inside a map value be written
on its own instead of rewriting the entry.

`#[app::state]` also emits two exports for the storage crate's merge of root
state, `__calimero_register_merge` and `__calimero_merge_root_state`. The
runtime calls the first when it loads the module; a cluster never merges root
state, so the second does not run there.

## Nested collection ids and the re-key pass

A collection constructed fresh — `Counter::new()`, `UnorderedMap::new()` — first
mints an `Id::random()`. That is fine for a *root*, but for a value placed inside
a map the id must instead be **derived from the map key**, so the value's
entities follow from where it is stored.

Two mechanisms cooperate:

- `compute_collection_id` derives the deterministic, key-based id for a
  collection placed inside a container.
- the **re-key pass** (`__assign_deterministic_ids()`) walks freshly-constructed
  values, moves each onto its deterministic key-derived id, and tombstones the
  random one it was born with.

This is why `#[app::init]` does not just return your state — the macro wraps it so
the re-key pass runs before the first commit:

```rust
// Generated by #[app::init] — your constructor is wrapped:
::calimero_storage::collections::Root::new(|| {
    let mut state = #call;            // your `init()` body
    state.__assign_deterministic_ids();
    state
})
```

The same wrapping runs for migrations (see below), so a migrated state's ids
follow from its keys too.

## Private storage: the caller's own space

`#[app::private]` marks a struct as state kept in the **caller's own private
space** ([Private storage](/build/host-functions/#private-storage)): replicated
and sealed with the rest of the app's state, but a run reads and writes only its
own caller's space, so no call can read another account's. You load it with
`T::private_load_or_default()` and mutate through an `EntryMut` guard
(`as_mut()`); the guard **auto-persists on `Drop`**, including on early
`?`-returns, so there is no explicit save call for the borsh-blob fields.

The `apps/private_data` app keeps each caller's plaintext secrets in their
private space and publishes only the hashes to shared state:

```rust
#[app::state(emits = for<'a> Event<'a>)]
pub struct SecretGame {
    games: AuthoredMap<String, LwwRegister<String>>, // shared: only hashes, each its creator's own
}

#[derive(BorshSerialize, BorshDeserialize, Debug)]
#[borsh(crate = "calimero_sdk::borsh")]
#[app::private]
pub struct Secrets {
    secrets: UnorderedMap<String, String>, // the caller's plaintext
    secrets_added: u64,
    // ...primitives, std collections, and tree-backed collections only
}
```

The macro **rejects at compile time** any field whose semantics assume the
shared state tree: CRDT types (`LwwRegister`, `Counter`, `GCounter`, `PNCounter`,
`ReplicatedGrowableArray`, `FugueText`, `RichText`, `RichDocument`), access-control collections (`SharedStorage`,
`UserStorage`, `FrozenStorage`), and authored collections (`AuthoredMap`,
`AuthoredVector`). A private space has exactly one writer — its account — so
none of them has anything to add. Use a plain `u64` / `String` / `Vec` instead.

:::caution[A public call and a handler have no private space]
A run with no caller account — a public call, or a handler or xcall, which runs
as an app — has no private space: reads find nothing and writes report failure. Keep in `#[app::private]` only what belongs
to one account; publish to `#[app::state]` what others need (here, the secret
*hashes*).
:::

:::caution[Type aliases defeat the private-storage rewrite]
To keep tree-backed collection fields in the private space, `#[app::private]`
injects `PrivateStorage` as the trailing generic on `UnorderedMap`,
`UnorderedSet`, `Vector` (and the sorted variants). It matches on the **last
path segment** of the type, so a fully-qualified path
(`calimero_storage::collections::UnorderedMap`) is covered — but a type alias or
`use … as` rename is **not**. An aliased collection silently keeps its default
`MainStorage`, and its entries land in the shared state every member can read,
defeating the whole point of `#[app::private]`. Write the collection type out by
name (or pass the explicit `PrivateStorage` parameter yourself); never reach a
private field through an alias.
:::

## `xcall`: fire-and-forget, node-gated, same organization

A cross-app call is **fire-and-forget**. `env::xcall(...)` does not invoke
anything inline — the host fn only **queues** the call, which is committed with
the originating entry as a follow-up and run **after** that entry commits, by
the target app's leader. The outcome never returns to the caller as a value.

```rust
pub fn ping(&mut self, target_context: ContextId) -> app::Result<()> {
    let params = serde_json::to_vec(&Params {
        from_context: ContextId::from(env::context_id()),
    })?;
    // Queues the call; dispatched after THIS execution commits.
    env::xcall(target_context.as_ref(), "pong", &params);
    Ok(())
}

#[app::xcall] // node gates this: an xcall to a non-#[app::xcall] method is denied
pub fn pong(&mut self, from_context: ContextId) -> app::Result<()> {
    // env::xcall_origin() is set by the NODE and cannot be forged.
    let Some(origin) = env::xcall_origin().map(ContextId::from) else {
        app::bail!("pong is xcall-only: a direct call carries no origin");
    };
    if origin != from_context {
        app::bail!("provenance mismatch: origin {} != claimed {}", origin, from_context);
    }
    self.counter.increment()?;
    Ok(())
}
```

Key properties:

- **Same organization.** The two apps must belong to the same organization, or,
  outside any organization, have the same owner.
- **`#[app::xcall]` gating is enforced by the node.** An xcall targeting a method
  without the attribute is refused before the method runs
  (`xcall denied: … is not an #[app::xcall] entry point`); a *direct* call to
  that method still works.
- **`env::xcall_origin()` is unforgeable.** The node sets it; the guest cannot.
  Use it to reject direct calls (no origin) and to verify a self-reported
  `from_context` against the real origin.

See [Handlers & cross-app calls](/protocol/xcall/) for how follow-ups are queued, run and bounded.

## Events with handlers

`app::emit!((event, "handler"))` attaches a handler name to an event. The handler
is a method on your state marked `#[app::handler]`, and the app's leader runs it
**once**, **after** the originating entry commits, as a call of the app itself:

```rust
pub fn set(&mut self, key: String, value: String) -> app::Result<()> {
    app::emit!((Event::Inserted { key: &key, value: &value }, "insert_handler"));
    self.items.insert(key, value.into())?;
    Ok(())
}

// Runs once, on the leader, after the entry that emitted the event commits.
#[app::handler]
pub fn insert_handler(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) -> app::Result<()> {
    self.handler_counter.increment()?;
    Ok(())
}
```

Only a method the app's embedded ABI declares a handler runs. An event naming
anything else, the SDK's own `__calimero_*` exports included, runs nothing. Any
caller can emit an event naming any declared handler with any arguments, so a
handler must check its input like any other entry point.

The handler is committed as a follow-up in the same entry as the event, so a
new leader picks up exactly the handlers still pending: none is skipped and none
runs twice. A handler that fails is recorded with its error and **not retried**,
so keep it to state changes that can stand on their own. Handlers and xcalls
chain at most 3 deep ([Limits](/protocol/limits/)).

## Migrations

A schema change is expressed with `#[app::migrate]` (a free function returning the
new state) or `#[derive(Migrate)]` (per-field rules), optionally guarded by
`#[app::migration_check]`. The leader runs it once, during the upgrade entry,
and the other replicas apply the state it wrote
([Upgrades & migrations](/protocol/upgrades/)). Still, **write a migrate as a
pure function of the old state**: the SDK refuses non-deterministic calls inside
it (below).

```rust
#[app::migrate]
pub fn migrate_v1_to_v2() -> ScenarioCrdtNativeV2 {
    // read_raw() returns the raw committed bytes of the old root,
    // with the trailing 32-byte Element id already stripped.
    let old_bytes = read_raw().expect("no existing state to migrate");
    let old: ScenarioCrdtNativeV1 =
        BorshDeserialize::deserialize(&mut &old_bytes[..]).expect("V1 decode");

    ScenarioCrdtNativeV2 {
        items: old.items,   // carry collections across unchanged
        title: old.title,
        tags: Vector::new(), // seeded purely from `old`, never from node state
    }
}
```

Two things the SDK runs around your migrate: `#[app::migrate]` executes under
storage **merge mode** (which zeroes identity and timestamp stamps), and the
generated wrapper calls
`__assign_deterministic_ids()` on the produced state — the same re-key pass as
`#[app::init]` — so freshly-seeded collections get position/key-derived ids
instead of `Id::random()`.

:::caution[`Counter::increment()` panics inside a migrate]
`increment()` stamps the executor's id into the counter's slots. Inside a
migrate it detects merge mode and **panics** loudly. If you must touch a counter in a
migrate, carry it across unchanged (`counter: old.counter`) or use
`increment_for(id)` with an explicit id.
:::

`#[derive(Migrate)]` expresses the same thing declaratively, with a per-field
strategy:

| Strategy | Syntax | Meaning |
|----------|--------|---------|
| carry | *(default)* | take the field from the old state unchanged |
| new | `#[migrate(new = EXPR)]` | field is new in this version; initialize with `EXPR` |
| from | `#[migrate(from = old_field)]` | renamed; pull from a differently-named old field |
| with | `#[migrate(from = f, with = func)]` | transform the old field through `func` |

```rust
#[app::state(version = 5, emits = for<'a> Event<'a>)]
#[derive(app::Migrate)]
#[migrate(from = MigrationSuiteV4, emit = Event::Migrated { /* ... */ })]
pub struct MigrationSuiteV5ChangeType {
    items: UnorderedMap<String, LwwRegister<String>>, // carry (default)
    details: LwwRegister<String>,                      // carry
    #[migrate(from = counter, with = counter_u64_to_string)]
    counter: LwwRegister<String>,                      // type change via fn
}
```

`#[app::migration_check]` is a `fn(old, new) -> bool` predicate the runtime runs
*before* committing the migration; returning `false` aborts. The check receives
the still-committed old root and the produced-but-uncommitted new root, so you can
assert invariants like entity-count parity. The witness it relies on is transient
— it rides the `Outcome` side-channel and is not part of committed state.

## The ABI travels inside the bytecode

The app's state schema (the wasm-ABI manifest) is embedded as a wasm **custom
section** named `calimero_abi_v1`, so it ships *inside* the module bytes and is
covered by the same hash as the code. The schema therefore cannot
change independently of the code: any edit to the ABI is an edit to the wasm
blob's identity.

The two sides of that boundary fail in opposite directions on purpose:

- **Reads are validation-gated and fail-open.** Loading the embedded schema
  returns `None` if the section is absent *or* malformed *or* well-formed JSON
  that doesn't pass manifest validation (dangling refs, bad state root). A
  missing schema doesn't brick a module — pre-schema modules simply get the
  default (write-lock, no downgrade check) behaviour.
- **Writes fail-closed.** Embedding the schema (build-time tooling) refuses a
  malformed or truncated module rather than emitting a corrupt one.

### The identity-downgrade rail

The node's upgrade planning (and the `cargo mero abi diff` CI lint) compare the old and
new manifests to catch a class of silent ACL-stripping upgrades. The
access-controlled wrappers — `PermissionedStorage` / `Ownable` / `AccessControl`
(and `SharedStorage`) — all normalize in the ABI to a collection carrying
`crdt_type = SharedStorage` plus the inner type, so their writer-set ACL is
*visible* in the schema. Swapping such a field to a plain, ungated type (say
`UnorderedMap`) strips its write rule from the app, and surfacing the wrapper as a
distinct shape is what makes the downgrade diff able to see it.

:::caution[The downgrade check fails closed on unresolvable types]
When the gate resolves a field's top-level type, an **unresolvable** type — a
reference cycle, a dangling `$ref`, or an unknown `crdt_type` — is *not* graded
as "plain". Folding it into "plain" would let an identity-gated field hidden
behind a broken ref slip past the gate as a missed downgrade. So an old field
that's gated-or-unknown is always compared against its new shape, and an
unresolvable new type reads as a downgrade. The only carve-out is when *both*
old and new are unresolvable and unchanged — a legacy app that has always had a
dangling ref and never used gated state.
:::

## Multi-service bundles

A bundle is usually one WASM module — the manifest's top-level `wasm` (+ optional
`abi`). It can instead carry several named modules in a `services` array, each a
`{name, wasm, abi?}` record. When `services` is present and non-empty it
**overrides** the single-service fields: the node ignores top-level `wasm` / `abi`
and installs one blob per service (`crates/bundle/src/lib.rs`).

A multi-service application stores those blobs in a `services` map keyed by name, and
an app instance runs exactly one of them. Select it with `--service` when you
create or upgrade it:

```text
meroctl context create --name <name> --package <package> --service <service>
```

At resolve time a `None` selection is only unambiguous for a single-service app or a
bundle with exactly one service; a true multi-service bundle (more than one entry)
requires the service name, otherwise the blob cannot be resolved
(`Application::resolve_service_blob`, `crates/primitives/src/application.rs`).

## Miscellaneous power facts

A grab-bag of things that are easy to get wrong:

| Concept | What to know |
|---------|--------------|
| `account_id` vs `device_id` vs `context_id` vs `xcall_origin` | `env::account_id()` is *who* is calling (a person; the same across their passkeys). `env::device_id()` and `env::executor_id()` return the same account: there are no per-device keys. `env::context_id()` is the current app. `env::xcall_origin()` is the node-set, unforgeable origin of an xcall (`None` for a direct call). |
| `app::Result` / `app::Error` | `Error` wraps a `serde_json::Value`, has a blanket `From` for any `std::error::Error`, and the `app::bail!` / `app::err!` macros build/return it. `?` on any std error just works. |
| view vs mutate | Only a `&mut self` method (or `#[app::init]`) commits state. A `&self` method **never** commits, even if it is not marked `#[app::view]` — so a missing `view` attribute is a missed optimization, not a correctness bug. |
| `TestHost` limits | Operations with no in-process implementation panic: `xcall`, `ed25519_verify`, and networked blob ops are unsupported. Event handlers are captured but **not** auto-dispatched (call them directly in tests). The default identity passes owner/access checks. |

For the runtime mechanics behind these, see [Handlers & cross-app calls](/protocol/xcall/) and
[CRDT collections](/protocol/crdt-internals/).
